newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Advancing rebels claim scalp of Zaire PM.
newsitem.headline: Advancing rebels claim scalp of Zaire PM.

text.p: Zaire's advancing rebels have claimed their biggest political scalp so far, forcing the resignation of President Mobutu Sese Seko's prime minister.
After five months of apparently unstoppable rebel successes in the east of the vast country, Kengo wa Dondo threw in the towel on Monday night.

The resignation plunged the capital Kinshasa into political uncertainty as hundreds of American, Belgian and French troops gathered across the mighty Zaire river in neighbouring Congo to prepare to evacuate foreign nationals.
The sizeable foreign force was mustering in Brazzaville with the stated mission of being ready to evacuate the estimated 7,000 Westerners living in Zaire.
"It is impossible for me to continue my task and therefore I resign," Kengo said in his letter of resignation to Mobutu.
The 66-year-old president, struggling against prostate cancer as well as Laurent Kabila's rebellion, accepted the letter but asked Kengo to remain in office until a successor was found.
A host of aspirants were jostling for the job but Etienne Tshisekedi, a longtime foe of Mobutu, was clearly the preferred candidate on the streets of Kinshasa.
Opposition parties were meeting on Tuesday to try to designate the new premier. Under Zaire's transitional constitution the opposition picks its choice but Mobutu must give his approval.
The paramount issue facing a new government is how to persuade Kabila to agree a ceasefire and enter negotiations.
Kabila, rejecting a U.N. ceasefire resolution, has said he will only stop fighting after the start of direct talks with Mobutu or Zaire's crumbling army.
Kengo, accusing Uganda and Rwanda of backing the rebels, had rejected any compromise but his pledge to whip the indisciplined army into shape proved empty.

The rebels, now in control of about one quarter of the country, are advancing on the vital Shaba region in the south whose colossal resources of copper, cobalt and precious metals make Zaire one of Africa's potentially richest countries.
Mobutu's MPR party signalled a major policy shift on Monday night, saying it now backed face-to-face talks with Kabila.
"The MPR thinks that direct negotiations with the rebels are very necessary. We are prepared to meet the devil himself to make peace and save lives," MPR vice-chairman Banza Mukalayi told Reuters.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen said on Monday that 219 U.S. troops were on standby near Zaire to evacuate American citizens and more than 600 troops should be in the area by Tuesday.
Other U.S. defence officials said the 219 American troops were in Brazzaville and in Gabon's capital Libreville.
Belgium began airlifting the first of 550 soldiers to Congo on Monday in operation "Green Stream", the sixth of its kind since Zaire won independence from Belgium in 1960.

"If necessary we'll stay in Brazzaville but I would prefer to get access to Kinshasa to help our nationals," Belgian Defence Minister Jean-Pol Poncelet told BRTN television. "The Americans and French have the same problem," he said.
Military sources in Paris said on Monday 300 French troops were in Brazzaville.
African efforts to mediate a solution to the Zaire crisis will begin on Tuesday in the West African state of Togo when foreign ministers meet ahead of a summit on Wednesday.
Kabila's aides said he would not attend the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) summit because of security fears in Togo, a close ally of Zaire's Mobutu.
But the rebels, invited to an OAU forum for the first time, were sending a senior delegation.

In Kinshasa, Mukalayi said Mobutu was still convalescing but would be represented by a three-man delegation: Andre Boboliko, a parliamentary vice-president and opposition supporter, Honore Ngbanda, Mobutu's security adviser, and Tshimbombo Mukuna, head of Zaire's intelligence services.
